title: Slope and Average Rate of Change
learningObjective: Determine the average rate of change of a given function over a given interval. Find the slope of a line.

faqs.question: What is average rate of change, and what does it actually measure?
faqs.answer: Average rate of change measures how much a function's output changes, on average, per unit of input, over a specific interval. Think of it like a road trip: if you drove 120 miles in 2 hours, your average speed was 60 mph — that doesn't mean you drove exactly 60 mph the whole time, just that on average, that's your rate. Average rate of change works the same way: it tells you the overall trend across an interval, not the behavior at every single instant.

faqs.question: What is the formula for average rate of change, and what do the parts mean?
faqs.answer:
The formula compares how much the output changed to how much the input changed, over the interval [a, b].
Formula

\[ \text{Average Rate of Change} = \dfrac{f(b)-f(a)}{b-a} \]

\( f(b) \) and \( f(a) \) are the y-values (outputs) at the two ends of the interval. \( b \) and \( a \) are the x-values (inputs). The numerator is the change in output; the denominator is the change in input.

faqs.question: What is slope, and how does it relate to average rate of change?
faqs.answer: Slope is a constant number that describes the steepness and direction of a line. For a linear function specifically, the average rate of change is always the same no matter which interval you pick — and that constant value is exactly what we call the slope. In other words: slope is just the average rate of change of a linear function, and it never changes.

faqs.question: Why does a linear function have a constant rate of change, but other functions don't?
faqs.answer:
A straight line rises (or falls) at exactly the same steepness everywhere along it — that's what makes it "straight." A curve, on the other hand, bends, so its steepness changes as you move along it — steeper in some places, flatter in others.

The teal line rises the same amount for every step right, no matter where you look. The orange curve is flatter on the left and steeper on the right.

faqs.question: What does it mean for slope to be positive or negative?
faqs.answer:
The sign of the slope tells you the direction of the line, reading left to right. A positive slope means the line rises as you move right — the function is increasing. A negative slope means the line falls as you move right — the function is decreasing. The size of the number (ignoring the sign) tells you the steepness; the sign alone tells you the direction.

Left to right: the teal line climbs (positive slope); the orange line falls (negative slope).

faqs.question: What is the slope formula, and where does it come from?
faqs.answer:
The slope formula is just the average rate of change formula, rewritten using point notation instead of function notation — same idea, different labels.
Formula

Given two points \( (x_1, y_1) \) and \( (x_2, y_2) \):

\[ m = \dfrac{y_2 - y_1}{x_2 - x_1} \]

This is "change in y" over "change in x" — or, informally, rise over run.

faqs.question: How do I calculate average rate of change from a table of values?
faqs.answer:
Pick your two endpoints from the table, and plug their x- and y-values into the average rate of change formula. You don't need any points in between — only the two endpoints of your interval matter.
Worked Example

Table: (−5, 28), (−4, 19), (−3, 12), (−2, 7)

Find the average rate of change from \( x=-5 \) to \( x=-2 \):

\[ \dfrac{f(-2)-f(-5)}{-2-(-5)} = \dfrac{7-28}{3} = \dfrac{-21}{3} = -7 \]

faqs.question: How do I calculate average rate of change from a graph?
faqs.answer:
Identify the two x-values that define your interval, find their corresponding y-values on the graph, then apply the formula exactly as you would with a table — the graph is just showing you the same (x, y) pairs visually.

Mark your two endpoints, then find the vertical distance (rise) and horizontal distance (run) between them.

faqs.question: How do I calculate average rate of change when I'm only given an equation?
faqs.answer:
Evaluate the function at both endpoints of the interval to get your two y-values, then plug everything into the formula — this is really just faq-2's formula in action.
Worked Example

Let \( f(x) = -3x^2 - 1 \). Find the average rate of change on \( [-2, 3] \).

\( f(-2) = -3(-2)^2-1 = -13 \)

\( f(3) = -3(3)^2-1 = -28 \)

\[ \dfrac{f(3)-f(-2)}{3-(-2)} = \dfrac{-28-(-13)}{5} = \dfrac{-15}{5} = -3 \]

faqs.question: Why do I get a different average rate of change depending on which interval I pick (for non-linear functions)?
faqs.answer: Because a curved graph's steepness genuinely changes from place to place, the "average steepness" you calculate depends entirely on which two points you choose. Pick an interval where the curve is steep, and you'll get a larger number; pick one where it's flatter, and you'll get a smaller number. This is completely expected for anything that isn't a straight line — it's actually one of the key differences between linear and non-linear functions.

faqs.question: Which point is (x₁, y₁) and which is (x₂, y₂) in the slope formula — does it matter?
faqs.answer:
It doesn't matter which point you call "first" and which you call "second" — but you do have to stay consistent within the same calculation. Whichever point you subtract first in the numerator, you must subtract that same point first in the denominator too. Swap both, and you'll get the exact same slope; swap just one, and you'll flip the sign by mistake.
Worked Example

Points: \( (-3, 7) \) and \( (7, 2) \)

Either order works: \( \dfrac{2-7}{7-(-3)} = \dfrac{-5}{10} = -\dfrac{1}{2} \)

or \( \dfrac{7-2}{-3-7} = \dfrac{5}{-10} = -\dfrac{1}{2} \) — same answer either way.

faqs.question: Why is the slope of a horizontal line 0, but the slope of a vertical line undefined?
faqs.answer:
A horizontal line has zero rise — the y-values never change no matter how far you move — so the numerator of the slope formula is 0, and 0 divided by anything is just 0. A vertical line has zero run — the x-values never change — so the denominator becomes 0, and division by zero is undefined. That's not a technicality; it reflects something real: a vertical line doesn't have a single steepness value at all.

Horizontal line (left): zero vertical change. Vertical line (right): zero horizontal change — division by zero.

faqs.question: What's the difference between "rise over run" and the slope formula — are they the same thing?
faqs.answer: They're the same idea, just two different ways to say it. "Rise over run" is the informal, visual version — count squares up/down and left/right on a graph. The slope formula, m = (y₂ − y₁)/(x₂ − x₁), is the precise algebraic version — it works even when you can't easily count grid squares, like when coordinates are fractions or decimals.

faqs.question: How do I interpret slope in a real-world context (like the thermostat example)?
faqs.answer: In context, slope tells you the rate something is changing per unit of whatever your input represents — usually time. If a house's temperature has a rate of change of −0.7 degrees per minute, that means the temperature is dropping seven-tenths of a degree every single minute. The sign tells you the direction (dropping vs. rising) and the number tells you how fast — always attach the units when you interpret slope in a real situation.

faqs.question: How does average rate of change here connect to what we'll see later with functions in general?
faqs.answer: Average rate of change is a tool you'll apply to every family of function you study from here on — polynomial, rational, exponential, trigonometric. Linear functions are simply the easiest case, since the rate of change never changes. As you move to more complex functions, you'll use this exact same formula to describe how fast they're growing or shrinking over any interval you choose.

faqs.question: Why does slope matter beyond just lines — where will this come back later in the course?
faqs.answer: Slope is your first exposure to one of the biggest ideas in all of mathematics: measuring how fast something changes. Later in calculus, this exact concept becomes the derivative — the instantaneous rate of change at a single point, rather than the average over an interval. Everything you're learning now about rise over run and average rate of change is quietly laying the foundation for that idea.

guided.title: Build Fluency with the AROC Formula
guided.prompt: I'm learning average rate of change in precalculus. Give me a function and an interval, and walk me through applying the formula (f(b)-f(a))/(b-a) step by step. Then give me three more practice problems of increasing difficulty — one from a table, one from a graph description, one from an equation — and check my work on each.

guided.title: Understand Why Linear Functions Are Special
guided.prompt: I'm learning that linear functions have a constant average rate of change but other functions don't. Can you show me this with a specific example — pick a linear function and a quadratic function, calculate the average rate of change over two or three different intervals for each, and help me see the pattern in the numbers?

guided.title: Practice the Slope Formula
guided.prompt: I'm practicing the slope formula m = (y2-y1)/(x2-x1). Give me pairs of points to practice with, including at least one pair that makes a horizontal line and one that makes a vertical line. Ask me to predict what will happen before I calculate, then check my reasoning.

guided.title: Debug Common Slope Mistakes
guided.prompt: I'm studying slope in precalculus. Can you show me three common mistakes students make with the slope formula — like mixing up which point is (x1,y1) vs (x2,y2), or mixing up when slope is zero vs undefined? For each mistake, show the wrong thinking, explain why it's wrong, and show the correct approach.

guided.title: Connect Slope to Calculus
guided.prompt: I just learned about average rate of change and slope in precalculus. I've heard this connects to something called the derivative in calculus. Without going too deep into calculus itself, can you explain in simple terms what that connection is, and why understanding average rate of change now will help me later?
